Divine Call
dih-VYN KAWL
noun phrase
From Latin divinus (of God, divine, from divus, god, deity) + Old English ceallian (to call, summon), related to Latin calare (to proclaim, summon). Divine call names the act of God by which He summons human beings to salvation and to service. Reformed theology distinguishes two forms: the general (external, outward) call that goes to all who hear the gospel, and the effectual (internal, inward) call that infallibly produces the response of saving faith in the elect.

Biblical Definition

The divine call is God’s sovereign summons to sinners, issued through the gospel. Reformed theology identifies two distinct modes. The general call (or external call) is the sincere offer of the gospel to all who hear it: God genuinely summons all to repent and believe (Matt. 11:28; Acts 17:30), and the rejection of this call increases human guilt. The effectual call (or internal call) is the Spirit’s inward work accompanying the gospel proclamation in the hearts of the elect: it convicts, illumines, draws, and regenerates, producing the faith it commands. Paul describes the effectual call as the second link in the golden chain of salvation: “those whom He predestined, He also called; and those whom He called, He also justified; and those whom He justified, He also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). The call in this chain is unfailing: every predestined person is infallibly called, and every effectually called person is infallibly justified and glorified. This is the irresistible grace of the Canons of Dort and the 1689 Baptist Confession (10.1). The divine call also encompasses the call to ministry: God sovereignly sets apart elders, deacons, missionaries, and teachers (Eph. 4:11), both through inward conviction and outward recognition by the church (Acts 13:2). In both senses—the call to salvation and the call to service—the initiative is wholly God’s: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with His Son” (1 Cor. 1:9). The called are not those who responded; they are those God’s sovereign grace drew irresistibly to Himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Divine call: God’s sovereign summoning of sinners to salvation through the gospel; in Reformed theology, distinguished as the general (external) call to all hearers and the effectual (internal) call to the elect that infallibly produces saving faith.

expand to see more

CALL, verb transitive. (Theology) To summon by the authority and power of God; to invite sinners to repentance and faith by the preaching of the gospel; in its special sense, to work effectually by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect, producing the faith and repentance the outward call commands.

DIVINE, adjective. Of God; proceeding from God; appropriately applied to any act, attribute, or work that originates wholly in the nature, purpose, and power of God rather than in human initiative or merit.

2. General call: the external offer of the gospel, issued to all who hear the Word preached; sincere in its terms, obligatory for all who receive it, and resistible by the hardened heart.

3. Effectual call: the inward work of the Holy Spirit by which the regenerate heart is drawn infallibly to Christ through the same preached Word that constitutes the general call; producing faith, repentance, and the beginning of the new life. The effectual call distinguishes the elect not by bypassing the Word but by opening the heart to receive it (Acts 16:14).

Key Scripture

2 Thessalonians 2:13 — "But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:"

2 Thessalonians 2:14 — "Whereunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ."

1 Corinthians 1:9 — "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord."

Romans 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Modern Corruption

Arminian theology collapses the distinction between the general call and the effectual call by making both resistible and conditioned on human response, effectively transferring the decisive cause of salvation from God’s sovereign choice to the sinner’s free cooperation.

expand to see more

The Arminian revision of the divine call holds that God calls all men effectually in the sense of providing sufficient grace for all, but that this grace is resistible and is made effective only by the sinner’s free cooperation. On this account, the decisive difference between the saved and the lost is not God’s sovereign effectual call but the human will’s free acceptance or rejection. The Reformed tradition rejects this at the root: Romans 8:30’s golden chain does not say “those whom He called, He hoped would respond”—it says those whom He called, He justified. The link is not conditional but causal and certain. If the effectual call depended on human cooperation, the chain would break wherever human wills rebel—which, given total depravity, would be always and everywhere. The effectual call must be monergistic (the Spirit alone as efficient cause) or it is not effectual.

A subtler corruption reduces the divine call to a subjective sense of vocation—the feeling that one is “called” to a profession, ministry, or lifestyle choice. The therapeutic culture has democratized “calling” into a self-discovery project: every individual is said to have a “calling” that personal reflection and a gifting inventory will reveal. This is not the divine call of Scripture, which is God’s sovereign act rooted in eternal election (2 Thess. 2:13), issued through the gospel (2 Thess. 2:14), and certified by the Spirit’s inward conviction. The call to ministry is validated not by private sentiment alone but by public recognition and formal ordination by the church (Acts 13:2–3; 1 Tim. 4:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin vocare (to call, summon) and Hebrew qara (to call, name, proclaim) converge on a sovereign divine act that runs through all Scripture: from God’s calling of Abraham out of Ur to His calling of the elect into fellowship with His Son.

expand to see more

Latin vocare / vocatio — to call, a calling; root of “vocation”—the divine call gives every legitimate form of human calling its theological ground: all work is a sphere in which God’s call is lived out

Hebrew qara — to call, proclaim, name; God’s calling of Abram (Gen. 12:1), of Israel by name (Isa. 43:1), of the servant (Isa. 49:1) establishes the OT pattern of sovereign summoning that the NT effectual call fulfills

Greek kletos — called; Paul’s self-description as “called to be an apostle” (Rom. 1:1) and his address to the Romans as “called to be saints” (Rom. 1:7)—both uses underscore that the called are defined by God’s act, not their response

Greek eklegō — to choose, elect; election and effectual call are inseparable in Paul (Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5; 2 Thess. 2:13)—the call is the temporal execution of the eternal decree of election

Latin efficax — effective, productive; the vocatio efficax (effectual call) distinguishes the Reformed from the Arminian account: an effectual call produces its intended effect without fail, by the Spirit’s sovereign work in the heart

Usage

"Westminster Confession 10.1 defines the effectual call: “All those whom God has predestinated unto life, and those only, he is pleased in his appointed and accepted time effectually to call, by his word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ.”"

"The distinction between the general and effectual call guards both the sincerity of the gospel offer (God genuinely calls all who hear) and the certainty of salvation (God’s effectual call cannot ultimately fail)—avoiding both the hyper-Calvinist reluctance to offer the gospel freely and the Arminian uncertainty about ultimate perseverance."

"Acts 16:14’s account of Lydia is the paradigm of the effectual call: Paul preached the general call; “the Lord opened her heart to respond to the things spoken by Paul”—the same outward word, but the Spirit’s inward operation making it effectual in one hearer."
